title: Subqueries & Correlated Subqueries
description: Distinguish scalar subqueries, subqueries with IN / EXISTS, and master correlated subqueries with planner optimization.

data.text: A **subquery** is a query nested inside another query. When a subquery executes independently of the outer query, it is an **uncorrelated subquery**. When a subquery references columns from the outer query, it is a **correlated subquery**.

A frequent optimization question is whether to use `IN (SELECT ...)` or `EXISTS (SELECT ...)`. In PostgreSQL, `EXISTS` terminates as soon as the first matching row is found (short-circuit evaluation), making it significantly faster for checking presence across large tables.

data.title: Optimized Membership Check with EXISTS
data.content: Notice the SELECT 1 inside EXISTS; it stops scanning upon first match.
data.code:
-- Efficient check for customers with at least one high-value order
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 
    FROM orders o 
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id 
      AND o.total_amount > 1000
);

data.title: The NOT IN with NULL Disaster
data.text: If any row in the subquery returns `NULL`, `NOT IN (SELECT col FROM ...)` evaluates to `UNKNOWN` for all outer rows and returns ZERO records! Always use `NOT EXISTS` instead of `NOT IN` to avoid this notorious SQL pitfall.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Correlated subqueries reference values from the outer query for each row.
Use `EXISTS` instead of `IN` when testing for presence to leverage short-circuit seeks.
Always prefer `NOT EXISTS` over `NOT IN` to prevent NULL-induced zero-result bugs.
